## [EvoScene-VLA: Recurrent Scene Prefix Boosts Chunked Robot Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21862) ⭐️ 8.0/10

EvoScene-VLA introduces a recurrent scene prefix that maintains an action-updated scene state across control chunks, combining current observations with prior action updates. On 31 RoboTwin tasks, it raises average success from 87.2% to 89.1% in fixed evaluation and from 86.1% to 88.5% in randomized evaluation, and outperforms all baselines on the Galaxea R1-Lite real robot. This addresses a key limitation in current VLA policies that rely solely on current visual observations, ignoring how actions alter the scene. By maintaining an action-updated scene prior, EvoScene-VLA improves robot control accuracy and robustness, potentially advancing real-world robotic manipulation. The recurrent scene prefix holds two groups of scene tokens: one from the current observation and one inherited from the previous chunk. During training, a Scene Predictor supplies future scene-token targets and Geometric Anchor aligns scene slots with frozen depth and 3D teachers, but both are discarded at deployment.

**Background**: Chunked vision-language-action (VLA) policies predict multi-step robot controls, conditioning each update on the current visual observation alone. However, robot actions cause contact, occlusion, and object motion, so the geometry that later decisions depend on can change before the next visual update arrives. Spatial VLAs improve current-frame geometry, while temporal VLAs aggregate past frames, but neither maintains an action-updated scene prior across chunks.

Periodic-TDL uses periodic Vietoris-Rips complexes to encode interactions across adjacent repeating units under periodic boundary conditions, and the HSMP encoder propagates information from long-range interactions to covalent bonds. ## [Annealed Softmax Greedy Achieves Near-Optimal Bayes Regret in Many-Armed Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.31034) ⭐️ 8.0/10

This paper proves that annealed softmax greedy achieves near-optimal Bayes regret in many-armed Bayesian Bernoulli bandits, specifically O~(m + T/m) and O~(√T) when m = Θ(√T). This provides a theoretical explanation for the effectiveness of uncertainty-agnostic updates in reinforcement learning. This result offers a theoretical foundation for why simple, uncertainty-agnostic policy updates (like those used in RLVR) can work well, potentially guiding the design of more efficient RL algorithms. It also clarifies the conditions under which such methods are near-optimal, which is valuable for both theory and practice. The proof relies on a linear upper-tail condition on the prior, which implies an abundance of near-optimal arms, ensuring that softmax leakage mostly lands on near-optimal arms. Simulations show that prior-anchored variants of greedy and annealed softmax, which use Beta posterior means and skip forced initialization, outperform baselines including Thompson Sampling when the number of arms is large.

**Background**: Multi-armed bandits are a classic framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, balancing exploration and exploitation. Bayesian regret measures the expected difference between a strategy's cumulative reward and that of the optimal strategy in hindsight. Annealed softmax greedy selects actions using a softmax over empirical mean rewards with a decreasing temperature, differing from greedy by placing some probability on non-best arms.

## [LatentSkill: Turning Textual Skills into LoRA Adapters for Efficient LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06087) ⭐️ 8.0/10

LatentSkill introduces a framework that uses a pretrained hypernetwork to convert textual skills into LoRA adapters, storing skill knowledge in weight space instead of context space. On ALFWorld and Search-QA, it outperforms in-context skill baselines while using significantly fewer prefill tokens. This approach reduces per-step token usage and improves agent performance, addressing context window limitations and privacy concerns associated with plaintext skill injection. It offers a modular and efficient way to extend LLM agents, potentially impacting real-world deployment where cost and privacy are critical. LatentSkill improves ALFWorld success by 21.4 and 13.4 points on seen and unseen splits with 63.9% fewer prefill tokens on average, and improves Search-QA exact match by 3.0 points while using 71.8% fewer tokens per step. The generated skill LoRAs exhibit structured semantic geometry, can be modulated via the LoRA scaling coefficient, and can be composed through parameter-space arithmetic.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 18, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents often use textual skills to encode reusable procedures, but injecting them into prompts at every step incurs high context overhead and exposes skill content as plaintext. LoRA adapters are a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that represents task-specific updates as low-rank matrices, while hypernetworks generate the weights of another network. ALFWorld is a text-based embodied AI benchmark for household tasks, and Search-QA is a question-answering benchmark.

## [MO-PQUCB: Hybrid Algorithm for Multi-Objective Bandits with Conversational Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08410) ⭐️ 8.0/10

This paper introduces MO-PQUCB, a hybrid algorithm that integrates proactive conversational queries with bandit feedback for multi-objective decision-making. It proves that proactive queries accelerate preference estimation and improve regret scaling over prior methods, and it characterizes statistical limits under corrupted queries. This work addresses a fundamental limitation in preference learning for multi-objective bandits by leveraging structured conversational signals, which are common in real-world interactive systems. The theoretical guarantees and robust estimator could improve the efficiency and reliability of personalized decision-making systems, such as recommender systems and interactive AI assistants. The algorithm uses shift-invariant regularization and dual-exploration UCB to combine query-based preference anchoring with bandit feedback. It models user queries via a Plackett-Luce subset choice model and shows that query-only learning suffers from a shift-invariance barrier, necessitating the hybrid approach.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 18, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-objective bandits extend the classical multi-armed bandit problem to settings where each arm yields a vector of rewards across multiple objectives, and the learner must balance these objectives according to unknown user preferences. The Plackett-Luce model is a statistical model for ranking or subset choice, often used to infer preferences from pairwise or subset comparisons. The shift-invariance barrier refers to the identifiability issue where certain transformations of preference parameters yield the same observed choice probabilities, making it impossible to learn preferences from query data alone.

SL-S4Wave introduces a self-supervised learning framework that combines contrastive learning with a structured state space model (S4) encoder, featuring multi-layer global convolution with multiscale subkernels to capture both local and long-range dependencies in multichannel physiological waveforms. The method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in arrhythmia detection and EEG tasks, showing strong label efficiency and cross-domain generalization. This work addresses a critical challenge in medical time series analysis by enabling effective representation learning from unlabeled physiological waveforms, which are abundant but often lack annotations. It could significantly reduce the need for labeled medical data, accelerate model development for arrhythmia detection and other physiological monitoring, and potentially improve clinical decision support systems. The encoder uses multi-layer global convolution with multiscale subkernels to capture fine-grained local patterns and long-range temporal dependencies. Experiments show consistent outperformance over supervised and self-supervised baselines in arrhythmia detection, high performance with fewer labeled examples, robustness on long waveform segments, and effective transfer to unseen arrhythmia types; it also generalizes to EEG tasks.

## [Statistical Adversaries: Natural Backdoor-like Features in Clean Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05516) ⭐️ 8.0/10

This paper reveals that clean vision datasets like ImageNet contain natural statistical signals that can act as backdoor-like adversarial triggers, transferring across models and suggesting inherent vulnerabilities in dataset structure. This finding challenges the assumption that adversarial vulnerabilities only arise from malicious poisoning or model-specific flaws, highlighting that ordinary datasets may harbor latent attack surfaces. It has broad implications for dataset auditing, model robustness, and security in computer vision. The researchers analyzed ImageNet to identify patterns strongly linked to specific labels, then applied statistical controls to remove random correlations. They demonstrated that these statistical adversaries are more targeted than generic corruptions and transfer across different model architectures.

## [Cross-Model Consensus as a Free Verifier for LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10139) ⭐️ 8.0/10

This paper introduces cross-model consensus, a training-free method for selecting correct reasoning chains in LLMs, where a panel of independently trained models vote on final answers. It outperforms self-consistency and self-scoring across seven benchmarks, and matches or beats trained reward models outside their training domain. This work offers a free and effective alternative to expensive reward models for test-time scaling, potentially reducing the need for labeled data and improving generalization. It could make LLM reasoning more reliable and accessible, especially in domains where trained verifiers are unavailable. The method relies on error decorrelation: independently trained models make different mistakes, so wrong answers scatter while the correct one accumulates agreement. The paper derives a parameter-free law predicting consensus accuracy from three panel statistics (mean absolute error 0.03) and identifies a shared-error floor where models share misconceptions.

**Background**: Test-time scaling improves LLM reasoning by generating multiple candidate chains and selecting the best one. Standard selectors include self-consistency (majority vote within one model) and trained reward models (which require labeled data and may not generalize). Cross-model consensus uses agreement across different models as a free verification signal.

## [Multimodal LLM Benchmarked on NRC Reactor Operator Exam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22067) ⭐️ 8.0/10

This paper evaluates the open-weight 31B multimodal model Gemma 4 31B-IT on the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission Reactor Operator Generic Fundamentals Examination (GFE), testing eight configurations that combine base model, SFT, RAFT, and different retrieval chunking strategies. Out of the box, the model answers 51.94% correctly and passes no papers, while SFT with fixed-size chunking retrieval passes 8 of 14 papers, reaching 80.23% on PWR items. This work is significant because it applies a rigorous, safety-critical benchmark (the NRC licensing exam) to a multimodal LLM, providing a realistic measure of domain competence. The findings highlight the importance of fine-tuning and retrieval strategies in specialized fields, and the result that the model approaches but does not reliably achieve operator-level command has implications for AI deployment in high-stakes environments. The evaluation set is a census of every GFE administered at the March sitting from 2015 to 2021, comprising seven PWR and seven BWR papers with 697 scored items. The preferred chunking granularity reverses with training state: structure-aware chunking is better before fine-tuning, while fixed-size chunking is better after, meaning chunking optimized for a base model cannot be inherited by its fine-tuned descendant. RAFT trails SFT by 2.2 to 2.3 percentage points overall, and the pipeline runs on a single workstation with no network access at run time.

## [WitCert: Sound Runtime Meter for KV-Cache Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28699) ⭐️ 8.0/10

WitCert introduces a provably sound runtime meter that provides per-(layer, head, step) upper bounds on the total variation between exact and compressed attention, enabling real-time detection of KV-cache quantization errors in LLM serving. It integrates with SGLang via an env-guarded patch and includes machine-checked proofs in Lean 4 for its core theorems. This addresses a critical gap in deployed LLM serving systems, where KV-cache quantization is typically validated only by offline benchmarks, leaving runtime degradation undetected. By enabling sound runtime observability and gating, WitCert can improve the reliability and quality of LLM serving, potentially benefiting production systems that rely on aggressive quantization for memory efficiency. The meter has two tiers: a deterministic band-norm-witness bound that is sound for any cache-preserving black-box quantizer and any query, and a tighter probabilistic certificate for a controlled subtractively-dithered INT8 quantizer under an explicit request-level failure budget. In experiments, meter-driven gating restored raw-cast fp8 quality from 22.8 to 79.7 on hard RULER tasks, and the certified int8 cache served 1.88× more KV tokens at the same memory in SGLang.

This paper identifies and formalizes simulator collapse in multi-agent RL, where training against a single LLM simulator leads to overfitting and poor generalization. It proposes two solutions: Verbalized Sampling (inference-time) and Co-Training (training-time), validated on three benchmarks with up to 14% improvement in held-out success. Verbalized Sampling broadens the simulator's behavior by sampling from a verbalized response distribution, reducing mode collapse. Co-Training jointly optimizes the policy against a population of trainable simulators, preventing overfitting to any single simulator's mode. Both solutions preserve policy diversity, and the human study confirms gains on real users.

## [KL Divergence Gating for Principled Communication in Multi-Agent RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14559) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces a novel gating mechanism for communication in multi-agent reinforcement learning, where agents communicate only when the KL divergence between their learned belief distributions exceeds a fixed threshold. This replaces the high-variance REINFORCE-based gating used in prior work like IC3Net. The approach addresses the instability and uninterpretability of REINFORCE-based gating, offering a principled alternative that could improve coordination in multi-agent systems. Empirical results show performance gains on harder benchmarks, suggesting potential for broader adoption in multi-agent RL. The method uses a softmax over LSTM hidden states to compute belief distributions over latent world states. On the Predator-Prey 20x20 benchmark, a threshold of epsilon=0.5 achieved 73.84 average steps and 42% success rate, outperforming IC3Net's 75.31 steps and 31% success rate, with tighter variance. On MPE simple_spread, the belief head improved mean reward by 12 points and reduced variance by 26x even when gating was inactive.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 18, 04:00

**Background**: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, communication is crucial for coordination, but deciding when to communicate is challenging. Existing methods either communicate at every timestep or learn a binary gate using REINFORCE, which suffers from high variance and instability. KL divergence measures the difference between probability distributions, providing a natural criterion for belief disagreement. This paper leverages that to create a more stable and interpretable gating mechanism.

## [Open-Source LLM Routers Fail to Beat Simple Baselines in Hybrid Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14641) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper presents a common measurement protocol and hybrid evaluation of four open-source model routers across RouterBench, BFCL v4, tau2-bench, and WebArena, testing 290 frozen tasks against a locked matrix of 2,610 candidate outcomes. The study finds that most routers perform similarly to simple baselines, with only vLLM Semantic Router varying with prompt content, yet it does not achieve the highest success rate on any benchmark. This finding is significant for the LLM routing community because it challenges the assumed benefits of sophisticated routing mechanisms, suggesting that many open-source routers may not offer practical advantages over simple heuristics. It underscores the need for standardized evaluation protocols and the inclusion of fixed-tier baselines to accurately measure router performance, potentially influencing future router development and benchmarking practices. Three of the four routers emit constant or near-constant tier assignments, while only vLLM Semantic Router varies materially with prompt content. Always-Mid matches Aurelio exactly on three benchmarks and within 0.003 on the fourth, and for vLLM, task-level superiority tests detect no task-specific advantage over a share-matched content-blind allocation, with equivalence established only on WebArena at the five-percentage-point margin.

This paper introduces AViD Journal, a pipeline that formalizes LaTeX mathematical statements in Lean 4 and issues a novelty verdict using a decision tree over three dimensions: prior existence in formal and informal corpora, non-triviality via automatic tactics, and structural proof distance measured by Jaccard distance over premise sets. Evaluation on withdrawn arXiv papers revealed three practical obstacles, including the gap between Lean compilation and semantic fidelity. This work addresses a critical gap in AI for mathematics: verifying novelty beyond mere correctness. It provides a concrete pipeline and highlights limitations, which could guide future research in automated theorem proving and mathematical knowledge management. The pipeline uses Mathlib as the formal corpus and TheoremSearch and Matlas as informal corpora, with a temporal filter and an LLM judge. The three obstacles identified are: successful Lean compilation does not guarantee semantic fidelity, recall is limited by theorem index coverage rather than the similarity metric, and arXiv removes source code of withdrawn papers, hindering benchmark reproducibility.

## [Synchronized Logit Steering Enables Prompt-Agnostic Steganography in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14697) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Synchronized Logit Steering (SLS), a deterministic steganographic scheme for large language models that derives a proxy prompt from the generated output itself, eliminating the need for sender and receiver to share the original prompt context. The method achieves 0.20 bits per token with a periodic-burst variant, roughly 10x the capacity of single-payload encoding. This advancement makes covert communication through LLMs practical in real-world scenarios where prompts are not shared, such as retrieval-augmented generation or proprietary systems. It has significant implications for security and privacy, enabling hidden message embedding that is statistically difficult to detect. SLS encodes payload values as token ranks within high-entropy regions of the proxy prompt distribution. Across ShareGPT, GSM8K, and SWE-bench Verified, the KL divergence between true and proxy prompt distributions falls below 0.5 nats once the synchronization window reaches 40 tokens, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests confirm outputs are statistically indistinguishable from greedy generations.

**Background**: Steganography in large language models embeds hidden messages within natural-sounding text. Existing token and logit-level methods typically require sender and receiver to share an identical prompt context, which is rarely guaranteed in production pipelines. SLS overcomes this by deriving a proxy prompt from the output, allowing both parties to reconstruct the same logit distribution without access to the original prompt.

## [Skill Loading Strategies Compared: Hybrid Cuts Token Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14943) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper systematically compares four content-preserving skill-loading methods for AI agents—Full, Skill Block, Reference, and Hybrid—across five benchmarks. It finds that conditional loading (Hybrid) reduces input tokens by up to 39.8% on SpreadsheetBench and achieves substantial reductions on large multi-turn skills, with no detectable quality loss. Token costs are a major operational expense for LLM-based agents, and this research offers practical guidance on reducing them without sacrificing performance. The findings are directly relevant to developers building efficient agent systems, especially those handling large, multi-turn skills. The study uses cache-correct effective input token usage for multi-turn tasks, which accounts for prompt caching. Results show no universal winner; ALFWorld gains are smaller because its procedures are short and repeatedly needed, and paired outcome tests do not establish equivalence despite detecting no quality differences.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 18, 04:00

**Background**: AI agents often inject full skill descriptions into every request, leading to high token usage. Progressive disclosure is a technique where skills are loaded on demand, reducing unnecessary context. This paper compares such conditional loading against full injection and other methods, using benchmarks like SearchQA and ScienceWorld to measure token efficiency and quality.

## [Influence Calibration for On-Policy Self-Distillation in Agentic RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14945) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces Influence Calibration for Self-Distillation (ICSD), a method that addresses the trust-utility mismatch in on-policy self-distillation by measuring the first-order response of each token's RL surrogate contribution to a teacher-directed perturbation. ICSD improves performance across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA under GRPO and GiGPO, achieving 96.1% ALFWorld success and a WebShop score of 93.1 at 7B scale. This work addresses a fundamental limitation in on-policy self-distillation for agentic reinforcement learning, where teacher trust alone does not align with the policy's optimization objective. By introducing influence calibration, it provides a more principled way to allocate token-level supervision, potentially improving the efficiency and effectiveness of training language agents for complex tasks. ICSD computes a first-order response of the importance-weighted RL surrogate contribution to a teacher-directed output perturbation, then applies batch-adaptive calibration to convert this non-stationary signal into bounded allocation weights while preserving the original auxiliary-loss mass per action turn. The method requires no additional model pass and only affects the distillation loss. Frozen-batch analyses show a reduction in teacher-supported mass assigned to objective-opposed tokens from 60.1% to 37.8% and an increase in cosine compatibility with the RL gradient by 0.192.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 18, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a training strategy where a language model acts as both teacher and student, using its own rollouts to generate token-level supervision. In agentic reinforcement learning, models are trained to perform multi-step tasks by interacting with environments, and OPSD provides dense supervision to guide learning. However, existing methods allocate supervision based on teacher trust, which may not align with the policy's actual objective, leading to suboptimal performance.

## [Attention Gathers Latent Variables, Not a Gate, in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15022) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper tests whether a gating mechanism admits latent variables into verbalizable form in language models, finding no such gate and instead evidence for a shared linear map decoding the variable across contexts. Using Jacobian lenses on a five-arm benchmark, the authors show that attention-mediated gathering inside a mid-depth window produces the readable form. This challenges the 'workspace' metaphor that suggests a gate controls access to verbalizable representations, offering a more nuanced view of how latent variables become reportable. It could influence future interpretability research and model design by shifting focus from gating to attention-based gathering mechanisms. The study uses Jacobian lenses on open-weight models and finds that demand raises a concept's lens visibility by +0.050 in percentile rank, with a shared linear map decoding the variable at 6.4-9.0x its selection-corrected floor. The effect localizes to a mid-depth window, with transport at least 17x above shallower layers under non-saturating readouts, and the window is demand-specific, concentrating sevenfold less when the variable is unused.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 18, 04:00

**Background**: The Jacobian lens is an interpretability technique that reads out what an internal activation is disposed to make the model say by linearly transporting residual-stream vectors into the final-layer basis. The 'workspace' metaphor in language model interpretability suggests that certain representations become verbally accessible through a gating mechanism, but this paper provides evidence against such a gate, instead supporting attention-mediated gathering.

## [ReForge: LLM-Driven Continual Adaptation of ABR Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15138) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ReForge is a new continual heuristic learning framework that uses a large language model (LLM) to iteratively edit a single page of fuzzy rules for adaptive bitrate (ABR) algorithms. Each edit is verified by replaying all past network scenarios, ensuring no regression, and the framework adapts to new scenarios in minutes. This work addresses a critical limitation of current ABR algorithms: they are designed for a fixed network scenario and fail when conditions change. The framework separates task-specific features from shared representations via policy-driven multi-path routing, and uses a column-stochastic consensus matrix calibrated by task affinities to block mismatched parameter updates. A unified Lyapunov drift analysis reveals a U-shaped trade-off between variance reduction and structural OCB, leading to a closed-form expression for optimal aggregation depth. TwinGridShield introduces a model-independent runtime authorization layer that validates LLM-generated grid commands against a deterministic network twin before execution. The paper introduces a polynomial-time decision procedure to determine whether a context-dependent argumentation framework (CDAF) can be reduced to a value-based argumentation framework (VAF). This work clarifies the expressive relationship between two important argumentation frameworks, potentially simplifying analysis and enabling more efficient reasoning in AI systems. It also provides complexity results that guide future research on context-dependent defeat. The decision procedure runs in polynomial time for the basic reduction question, but neighboring problems have upper bounds ranging from NP to Sigma^p_3. The reference implementation validates the theoretical findings and shows that representability decreases rapidly with the number of contexts.

Context-dependent argumentation frameworks (CDAFs) instead let the context determine which attacks succeed, without explicit values.

VARM-Bench introduces a benchmark for Chinese abusive speech moderation with field-anchored chain-of-thought rationales and a deterministic evaluation protocol. It evaluates language models across multiple families using zero-shot prompting, taxonomy guidance, and structured CoT supervision. This benchmark addresses a gap in existing Chinese abusive speech benchmarks by providing a unified representation for deterministic verification of moderation decisions. It reveals that strong label-level performance can conceal substantial errors in complete moderation records, which is crucial for AI safety and reliable content moderation. Each instance in VARM-Bench includes a natural-language rationale with explicit anchors for six decisions: target, target type, target explicitness, author stance, harmfulness label, and fine-grained category. The deterministic protocol evaluates field correctness, target alignment, output validity, complete-record agreement, and hidden record errors without relying on an LLM judge.

**Background**: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning involves generating intermediate steps to arrive at a final answer, but traditional CoT may lack verifiability. Field-anchored CoT anchors each step to explicit, inspectable evidence, and deterministic evaluation uses rule-based methods to assess outputs without subjective LLM judges. This benchmark applies these concepts to Chinese abusive speech moderation, which is important for social media platforms.

## [BACE Framework Corrects Bias in Emotion Predictability Ceilings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15619) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces BACE (Bias-corrected Affective Ceiling Estimation), a framework that estimates a bias-corrected ceiling for emotion predictability from text, separating irreducible from reducible error. It uses an anchored Dirichlet-mixture empirical Bayes estimator and a claim gate to discipline saturation claims. This work addresses the underexplored question of whether emotion recognition accuracy has reached a ceiling, providing a rigorous method to quantify uncertainty in such claims. It could influence how saturation is reported in NLP benchmarks, promoting more disciplined evaluation across the field. Unconstrained point estimates of reachability range from 0.38 to 1.03, showing that saturation cannot be decided by any single estimator. The only assertion passing the claim gate is that at least about 33% of a representative classifier's error on GoEmotions is irreducible, with similar patterns on offensiveness and irony datasets.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 18, 04:00

**Background**: Emotion recognition from text is a common NLP task, but benchmarks often report improving accuracy without questioning whether a ceiling exists. Annotation noise and estimator choice can bias estimates of predictability, making it hard to know if further progress is possible. Fano's inequality provides an information-theoretic lower bound on error probability, which can be used to estimate ceilings. Empirical Bayes methods estimate priors from data, helping to correct for noise in annotations.

RLCascadeRouter is a new framework that formulates cascade routing for LLMs as a Markov decision process, using trajectory returns and advantages to directly optimize the performance-cost objective without relying on quality estimators. It outperforms strong baselines across ten LLMRouterBench benchmarks with thirteen LLMs. This work addresses a key limitation of existing cascade routing methods by eliminating the need for quality estimators, which can be inaccurate and lead to suboptimal routing decisions. It offers a more direct and potentially more effective approach to optimizing performance-cost trade-offs in LLM inference, which is crucial for practical deployment. The Cascade Policy Network models candidate complementarity for model selection and remaining-action value for stopping, eliminating independent post-hoc response-quality estimators. The framework can incorporate unseen models without retraining, and ablation studies validate both policy components.

RLCascadeRouter instead directly optimizes the routing decisions using reinforcement learning.

The paper introduces Gated Counterfactual Refinement for Communication (GCR-C), a rollout-style correction layer that improves reconstruction quality in generative visual-token communication by replacing baseline token selections only when a positive baseline-relative gain is predicted. This work addresses a critical limitation in generative visual-token communication by directly optimizing for reconstruction gain rather than relying on heuristic selection criteria. It demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple datasets and channel conditions, potentially enabling more efficient and reliable visual communication systems in bandwidth-constrained scenarios. GCR-C constructs a compact diversified candidate set, evaluates each candidate through matched full-budget Local-MDL continuation, and replaces the baseline action only when a positive baseline-relative reconstruction gain is obtained. Experiments on CIFAR-10, STL-10, a coded 5G-LDPC link, and a limited high-resolution Kodak transfer show consistent improvements at active low- and medium-rate operating points without increasing the realized packet rate, while revealing a quality-computation tradeoff.

ParaTempo introduces a training-free asynchronous parallel reasoning framework that uses a novel temporal confidence metric to dynamically prune, retire, fork, and stop reasoning branches. Experiments show it reduces latency by 21.8-32.2% and token usage by 18.1-30.3% while maintaining competitive accuracy. This addresses a key computational bottleneck in large reasoning models by enabling efficient parallel exploration without additional training. It could significantly reduce inference costs for complex reasoning tasks, benefiting both researchers and practitioners deploying such models. Temporal confidence is a branch-local measure of answer-space convergence, computed by probing each branch's tentative answer probability distribution over time. The framework operates asynchronously without synchronization among trajectories, and the metric shows stronger temporal stability and predictive power than token-level or instantaneous signals.

## [LAVA: Logic-Aware Framework for Auditable Financial Document Validation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16763) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LAVA is a new modular, backbone-agnostic pipeline for financial document auditing that integrates four stages: document-rule retrieval, layout-preserving information extraction, auxiliary metadata enrichment, and auditable symbolic/arithmetic verification. It outperforms baselines in hallucination control and edge-case handling while maintaining efficient token usage on a large real-world benchmark. This framework addresses the high-stakes need for accuracy, consistency, and reproducibility in financial document validation, such as payroll auditing, tax compliance, and loan underwriting. By enabling robust rule grounding and traceable execution, LAVA could improve trust and adoption of AI in finance, where errors are costly and auditability is critical. LAVA is evaluated on a large real-world benchmark with diverse financial documents and dozens of expert-curated validation rules, demonstrating practicality for high-volume, time-critical validation. The framework is backbone-agnostic, meaning it can work with various multimodal LLMs, and it emphasizes auditable symbolic/arithmetic verification to reduce hallucinations.

## [PIHF: Policy Iteration with Human Feedback for In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16831) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Policy Iteration with Human Feedback (PIHF), a method that integrates policy iteration with human feedback to iteratively improve language model policies for in-context learning. It was validated on ultra-rare-disease benchmarks, achieving significant Recall@1 gains across multiple executors. PIHF demonstrates a novel approach to post-training reinforcement learning that leverages fixed-weight language models as execution substrates, enabling expert-guided policy development without model fine-tuning. This could significantly impact clinical applications and other data-scarce domains where iterative improvement is crucial. The method uses a language-model critic and clinical expert to review reasoning and tool-use trajectories, localize failures, and form candidate revisions, with the expert retaining authority over admission and rollback. Across ablations, PIHF improved Recall@1 by 32.7 percentage points for GPT-5.4 and 31.1 points for Qwen3.6-35B, a difference of 1.7 points.

## [TRACE: A Temporal Reasoning Benchmark for LRMs with Difficulty Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.04784) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces TRACE, a testing framework that models temporal reasoning as constraint satisfaction problems using Allen's Interval Algebra, and constructs TRACEBench, a benchmark of 1,200 synthesized test instances across graded difficulty levels. It also incorporates a Trace-Based Verification Oracle to validate reasoning faithfulness. TRACE addresses critical limitations in current LRM benchmarks, such as data contamination and lack of fine-grained difficulty control, providing a more reliable evaluation of temporal reasoning capabilities. The framework's ability to expose reasoning flaws and spurious guessing could drive improvements in LRM reliability and transparency. The benchmark includes 1,200 synthesized test instances, and evaluations of eight LRMs show a strong negative correlation (Pearson's r ≈ -0.96) between performance and difficulty. The trace-based analysis reveals a spurious guessing rate of about 28% in mid-sized models, and identifies scale-dependent failure modes such as Degenerative Loops and Reasoning Explosion.

In real-vehicle tests with Autoware.Universe, native Orion failed due to GPU memory limits, but the hybrid version ran successfully alongside the full vehicle stack.

## [Uncertainty Fusion Fails to Beat Raw LLM in Legal Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14617) ⭐️ 7.0/10

An empirical study on 1,000 European Court of Human Rights cases found that fusing uncertainty tools (evidence graphs, Bayesian odds, Dempster-Shafer, conformal prediction) does not improve case-outcome prediction over using a frontier LLM directly. The pipeline's only benefit is operational: with conformal selective prediction, it achieves 96.8% accuracy on auto-cleared cases, but calibration error doubles when naively composing LLMs with Bayesian and Dempster-Shafer fusion. This negative result challenges common assumptions in legal AI that complex uncertainty fusion pipelines are necessary for reliable predictions. It suggests that frontier LLMs used directly are already strong discriminators, and the real value of such pipelines lies in calibrated trust and selective automation, not sharper prediction—an important insight for high-stakes legal applications. The study tested three families across two frontier LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5) on discrimination cases, finding AUROC around 0.83 with no improvement from the pipeline. Dempster-Shafer fusion was found to be unsafe on long chains, committing to wrong labels at below-chance accuracy, and the authors recommend removing it. After removing Dempster-Shafer and recalibrating, the tuned engine auto-clears at 96.8% accuracy with 0.5% errors escaping, versus 85.9% for an untuned baseline.

The paper introduces DeMTS, a framework that models the denoising trajectories of diffusion language models as multivariate time series over learnable latent variables, capturing token-step patterns to detect hallucinations. It outperforms existing methods on two D-LLM backbones and three benchmarks. This addresses a critical gap in hallucination detection for diffusion language models, which are an emerging alternative to autoregressive LLMs. By preserving the full two-dimensional token-step structure, DeMTS could improve reliability and safety of D-LLMs in real-world applications. DeMTS uses a trajectory-preserving token-to-variable assignment module to convert token signals into stable latent variables, then applies dynamic multivariate temporal modeling to integrate inter-variable dependencies with temporal encoding. The method demonstrates strong robustness, efficiency, and cross-task transferability.

## [FedImp: Impurity-Based Weighting Boosts Federated Learning Convergence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14654) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FedImp is a novel federated learning algorithm that assigns aggregation weights based on the informational content (impurity) of each device's local data. Experiments on EMNIST and CIFAR-10 show it reduces communication rounds by up to 66.7% compared to FedAvg, FedProx, and FedAdp, while achieving higher accuracy under highly imbalanced data. This addresses a core challenge in federated learning—non-IID data—which often slows convergence and degrades model performance. By improving convergence speed and accuracy, FedImp could make federated learning more practical for real-world applications with heterogeneous client data, reducing communication costs and enabling faster model updates. FedImp quantifies each device's contribution using impurity-based metrics (e.g., Gini impurity or entropy) and normalizes them to compute aggregation weights. The method was tested on EMNIST and CIFAR-10, showing communication round reductions of up to 64.4%, 27.8%, and 66.7% on EMNIST, and 44.2%, 44%, and 25.6% on CIFAR-10 compared to FedAvg, FedProx, and FedAdp, respectively.

## [DeCo-MIL: Counterfactual Reasoning for Long-Tailed WSI Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14719) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DeCo-MIL introduces a debiased counterfactual reasoning method to address nested dual long-tail distributions in whole slide image (WSI) analysis, improving rare-class recognition. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on three long-tailed WSI benchmarks. This work tackles a critical challenge in medical image analysis, where rare diseases are often underrepresented, leading to biased models. By improving rare-class recognition, DeCo-MIL could enhance diagnostic accuracy for less common conditions, benefiting both clinicians and patients. DeCo-MIL clusters patches into tissue-morphology anchors and applies counterfactual interventions by replacing each anchor with a normal prototype, estimating contributions with class-frequency-corrected predictions. It also constructs anchor-stratified pseudo-bags with tail-aware oversampling and consistency regularization to increase supervision for tail classes.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 18, 04:00

**Background**: Multiple instance learning (MIL) is a weakly supervised learning paradigm where data is organized into bags of instances, and a bag is labeled positive if at least one instance is positive. In whole slide image analysis, each slide is a bag of patches, and long-tailed distributions occur when some classes have far fewer examples, causing models to favor head classes. Counterfactual reasoning involves imagining alternative outcomes to understand causal effects, which DeCo-MIL uses to debias the model.

## [Tail-Aware Top-k On-Policy Distillation Improves LLM Accuracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14728) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Tail-Aware Top-k On-Policy Distillation (TA-OPD), a novel method that adds a tail token to the top-k tokens during on-policy distillation to restore tail probability information. This prevents the degradation in student model accuracy caused by top-k normalization, improving Avg@8 by up to 8.05 points on common benchmarks. This work addresses a critical limitation in on-policy distillation for language models, where ignoring tail probabilities can lead to increased entropy and degraded downstream performance. By providing a simple yet effective fix, TA-OPD could improve the quality of compressed models, making them more practical for deployment. TA-OPD minimizes reverse KL divergence over the top-k tokens plus an additional tail token that carries the total tail probability. The method is validated through extensive experiments, showing consistent improvements across benchmarks, and the code is publicly available at https://github.com/HuipengHuang/TA-OPD.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 18, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a technique where a student language model learns to match the teacher's next-token distribution along its own generated trajectories. To reduce computational cost, many methods only consider the teacher's top-k tokens and normalize their probabilities, but this discards the tail probability mass, which can cause the student's distribution to become more uniform and less accurate. TA-OPD addresses this by explicitly modeling the tail probability as a separate token, preserving the information needed for better alignment.

This paper introduces CF-ZOO, a novel method that provides counterfactual explanations for Pareto Conditioned Networks (PCNs) in multi-objective reinforcement learning. It searches for minimal changes to the desired-return command that would alter the policy's action, using a boundary-seeded directional search. This work addresses the opacity of PCN policies, enhancing interpretability and trust in multi-objective RL systems. It provides actionable explanations in terms of user preferences, which is crucial for debugging and real-world deployment where trade-offs matter. The method adapts adversarial machine learning techniques to RL explanations and introduces a boundary-seeded directional search that outperforms purely local optimization. It uses a return-only PCN variant to avoid ambiguity from horizon-conditioning, and the explanations are phrased as 'If your trade-off had shifted slightly towards X, the agent would have chosen Y.'

**Background**: Pareto Conditioned Networks (PCNs) are neural architectures that learn multiple policies for multi-objective reinforcement learning by conditioning on a desired return command. Counterfactual explanations in RL answer 'Why not?' or 'What if?' questions by identifying minimal changes to inputs that would alter the agent's action. This paper builds on these concepts to explain PCN decisions in the command space.

## [PAS-QFL: Personalized Ansatz Selection for Quantum Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14995) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PAS-QFL introduces a framework that decomposes each client's quantum neural network into a globally shared ansatz and a client-specific private ansatz, personalizing the structure of the private ansatz to handle data heterogeneity. Experiments show improved average Macro-F1 over fixed-ansatz QFL baselines. This work addresses a critical limitation in quantum federated learning by acknowledging that client data heterogeneity affects ansatz suitability. It could lead to more stable and fair QFL performance across diverse clients, advancing practical applications of quantum machine learning. The shared ansatz is selected via a stability-aware cross-client criterion, while the private ansatz is selected per client using local Macro-F1 to avoid misleading accuracy under class imbalance. Clients upload only shared parameters for aggregation, preserving personalization.

**Background**: Quantum federated learning (QFL) combines federated learning principles with quantum neural networks (QNNs) to enable collaborative training without sharing private data. In classical federated learning, non-IID data is a known challenge, and this paper extends that concern to QFL by personalizing ansatz structures.

## [SHOPCA: Curvature-Aware PCA for Geometric Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15313) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces SHOPCA, a novel PCA variant that regularizes the global covariance matrix with the mean shape operator, incorporating curvature information into dimensionality reduction. It also proposes an unsupervised criterion based on the spectral eigengap to select the mixing coefficient alpha without class labels. SHOPCA bridges differential geometry and classical PCA, offering a geometry-aware dimensionality reduction that consistently improves clustering quality over PCA on over 50 benchmark datasets. It outperforms UMAP in small-sample settings, making it valuable for unsupervised learning tasks where data is limited. The method uses a single trace-normalized mixing coefficient alpha, recovering standard PCA at alpha=0 and a curvature-driven embedding as alpha approaches infinity. The unsupervised alpha selection maximizes the relative eigengap between the top-d and remaining eigenvalues, and the method is computationally tractable and parameter-efficient.

AudioTQ introduces a novel lossy audio codec that operates directly in the time domain, using a randomized Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform (FWHT) rotation to uniformize amplitudes, followed by a 6-bit Lloyd-Max quantizer with a 1-bit QJL residual correction layer. It achieves up to 74.4% physical size reduction with an SQNR of ~30 dB, and is designed for real-time single-threaded CPU execution. This work challenges the traditional psychoacoustic and frequency-domain paradigm of audio codecs (e.g., MP3, AAC, Opus) by offering a data-oblivious, computationally simpler alternative inspired by LLM quantization. It could lead to more efficient audio compression on CPU-only devices, potentially impacting streaming, storage, and embedded systems. The codec packs 7-bit virtual indices into native 8-bit containers to align with CPU register boundaries, ensuring efficient single-threaded execution. The paper also analyzes the butterfly network of the FWHT and derives mathematical failure modes under sparse inputs, providing a thorough theoretical foundation.

This paper introduces invariant pretraining (InvPT), a code-only continued pretraining method that combines masked language modeling with multi-positive supervised contrastive learning to improve the robustness of encoder-based code representation models against syntactic variations. Across four baselines, two tasks, and four datasets, InvPT improves robustness by up to 11 percentage points on clone detection and 19 on code classification while maintaining or improving standard accuracy. This work addresses a critical robustness gap in widely deployed code representation models, which are used for tasks like clone detection and code classification. By providing a simple, code-only recipe that significantly improves robustness, it could enhance the reliability of AI-powered software engineering tools and inspire further research into invariant learning for code. InvPT applies semantic-preserving transformations to the corpus and treats all augmentations of the same source function as positives, mixing self-contrast pairs (same code, different masks) with invariant-contrast pairs (transformed code) for varying difficulty. Unlike prior contrastive code encoders, InvPT does not require paired natural-language data, and ablations show that multi-positive invariant contrast is the main source of gains.

## [Self-Verification Pipeline Catches Hallucinated Citations in Video-LLM QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15574) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces a self-verification pipeline that detects hallucinated timestamped citations in video-LLM question answering. It shows that direct verification fails due to sycophancy, while a small NLI model achieves a 79% catch rate on adversarial false-premise questions. This addresses a critical trust issue in video-LLM systems, where timestamped citations can mislead users into believing claims are grounded. The findings highlight the prevalence of sycophancy and offer a stable, interpretable verification method, potentially improving reliability of AI-generated video answers. The pipeline uses a retrieval-augmented language model to draft answers with per-claim timestamp citations, then independently re-examines each cited frame. Ablations show that direct vision-model verification catches 0% of 40 claims, blind re-captioning with a general LLM judge is unstable (0-100% flagged), and a small NLI model provides stable verification. The code is released for both Apple Silicon (MLX) and Google Colab (CUDA).

## [HAFR-Net: Progressive Refinement for VHR Image Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15647) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces HAFR-Net, a progressive refinement framework for very-high-resolution (VHR) remote sensing image segmentation, featuring Heterogeneity-Guided Stage-Adaptive Fusion (HG-SAF), a Frequency-Residual Adapter (FRA), and a Confusion-Aware Tri-Prior Decoder (CATP). Under a matched Swin-B training and single-scale inference protocol, it achieves 84.12%, 87.86%, 55.17%, and 67.70% mIoU on ISPRS Vaihingen, ISPRS Potsdam, LoveDA, and OpenEarthMap, improving the matched UPerNet baseline by 0.55, 0.95, 1.55, and 1.84 percentage points, respectively. HAFR-Net addresses a critical challenge in VHR remote sensing segmentation: effectively exploiting hierarchical features from pretrained encoders without disrupting them. Its consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks suggest it could become a strong baseline for future research in remote sensing and computer vision, particularly for applications requiring fine boundary and thin-structure accuracy. The HG-SAF module predicts dense stage weights conditioned on local feature variation, enabling adaptive fusion. The FRA injects frequency information via a bounded, zero-initialized residual branch, keeping the fused representation as reference. The CATP decoder regularizes predictions with boundary, objectness, and class-relation cues, and controlled analyses show improved boundary and thin-structure accuracy over matched alternatives.

The paper introduces RRFC, a framework that enables iterative refinement in image-to-image generation by feeding the model's own previous output back as auxiliary input channels, without redesigning the core architecture. This paper proposes a detection framework that monitors temporal consistency between a physical system and a potentially degraded digital twin to identify cyber-physical attacks. The framework combines a predictor trained on normal behavior, multi-horizon temporal features, unsupervised density modeling, and sequential change detection, achieving up to 98% detection reliability on SWaT with false alarm rates below 2%. This work is significant because it reframes digital twin degradation—often seen as a limitation—as a useful signal for security monitoring in cyber-physical systems. It offers a practical, unsupervised approach that does not require attack signatures or labeled attack data, making it applicable to real-world ICS environments where such data are scarce. The framework is evaluated on three ICS datasets: SWaT, HAI, and BATADAL, under multiple degradation scenarios including time desynchronization and partial observability loss. It detects attacks at the event level with bounded false alarm rates and low latency, and remains effective even when the digital twin view is degraded.

This paper introduces the concept of reliable-input selection for teledermatology, where the model picks the most reliably classifiable image among multiple photos of the same case. An oracle selector that chooses a correctly classified image when one exists raises weighted F1 by about 20 percentage points on average across six datasets and nine backbones. This addresses a practical problem in medical AI deployment, where distribution shifts cause misclassification. If reliable-input selection can be captured in practice, it could significantly improve the accuracy and trustworthiness of dermatology models in real-world teledermatology settings. The paper benchmarks four training-data-free selectors: embedding norm, neighborhood consensus, prediction stability under perturbations, and model confidence. None substantially narrow the oracle gap; the best is model confidence, but it recovers only a small part on clinical datasets. A small labeled reference set does not help much either, with the best fusion of confidence and Mahalanobis distance still leaving most of the gap.

STAIR follows a rule-first design, resolving standard questions without invoking an LLM and applying semantic adaptation only when the rule path fails. The best configuration, using balanced DDPM augmentation, improved accuracy from 84% to 88%, balanced accuracy from 67% to 81%, macro F1 from 65% to 78%, and recall for the underrepresented not-bombed class from 41% to 69%. ## [Ventor-QTest: Black-Box Audit Framework for Vendor-Hosted LLM APIs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16391) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Ventor-QTest is a composite black-box audit framework that verifies the fidelity of vendor-hosted LLM inference APIs without requiring internal probability information. It uses repeated-request and long-sequence probes to compute average fidelity loss (AFL) and extreme fidelity loss (EFL), respectively. This framework addresses the growing need to audit third-party LLM APIs, which are increasingly used but often opaque. By providing a statistical method to detect fidelity loss, it helps ensure reliability and trustworthiness in AI deployments, especially for long-horizon agentic tasks. AFL is a null-bias-corrected, within-window mean coarsened-KL statistic, while EFL uses the empirical upper tail of a run-level reference-centered-surprisal statistic. The framework showed strong linear agreement with logprob-derived coarsened-KL in three route conditions, and EFL correlated with declines in Terminal-Bench pass rates.

## [HarmTrace: Fine-Grained Target Identification in Harmful Memes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16622) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces a new task and dataset (Meme3W) for fine-grained target identification in harmful memes, along with a strict evaluation metric (JRA). It also proposes HarmTrace, an anchor-calibrated decoupled optimization framework that significantly improves JRA on multimodal LLMs, e.g., from 17.58% to 52.51% on Qwen3-VL-8B. This work extends harmful meme detection beyond binary classification to fine-grained target identification, which is crucial for understanding and mitigating online harm. It highlights the limitations of current multimodal LLMs and provides a framework to improve their performance, benefiting AI safety research and content moderation systems. Meme3W unifies multiple public harmful meme datasets with human-verified annotations for harmful instances. JRA requires the harmfulness label and all target-identification fields (target category, entity, textual mention, visual region) to be jointly correct. HarmTrace uses entity-aware supervised fine-tuning and Conditional Target-identification Policy Optimization (CTPO) with a Virtual Positive Anchor (VPA).

## [Study Finds Adding Explanations Often Boosts In-Context Learning Accuracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16627) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new comparative study evaluates how different sources and selection methods of natural language explanations (NLEs) affect downstream performance in in-context learning (ICL). The study finds that adding NLEs to few-shot prompts often improves accuracy over few-shot prompting without explanations, and that externally generated LLM explanations are competitive with human-written ones. This research provides empirical guidance for practitioners using explanation-augmented prompting in ICL, helping them choose effective explanation sources and selection strategies. It also highlights the potential of using LLM-generated explanations as a scalable alternative to costly human-written rationales. The study spans six benchmarks and four instruction-tuned models, comparing NLE sources (human-written, self-generated, and external LLM) and selection methods (random vs. faithfulness-based filtering). Results show that faithfulness-based selection yields small average gains but can vary by metric, task, and model, and different faithfulness metrics can disagree substantially.

The paper introduces UFFM, a novel semi-supervised semantic segmentation method for remote sensing that combines a unified training flow (UF) with a feature memory bank (FMB) to improve pseudo-label quality and reduce feature discrepancy between labeled and unlabeled data. The method integrates an external visual foundation model with a remote sensing domain teacher to generate less biased pseudo-labels. UFFM consists of two main innovations: the unified flow (UF) that jointly optimizes labeled and pseudo-labeled data under a unified training objective, and the feature memory bank (FMB) that dynamically updates class-specific features during training and aligns features between labeled and unlabeled data. The method was validated through extensive experiments on remote sensing datasets, showing superiority over state-of-the-art S4 methods, and the code is publicly available on GitHub.

## [MIRROR: Auditable Radiology Reports via Separated Classifier and Writer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16709) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MIRROR is a research prototype that chains a multi-label classifier, a Grad-CAM localizer, and a report writer that never sees the image, preventing the language model from asserting unmeasured findings. The system routes three modalities (chest X-ray, brain MRI, head CT) through a shared registry, with one modality trained and tested on ChestMNIST. This architecture addresses a critical problem in medical AI: hallucinated findings in radiology reports. By making findings auditable against the probability vector, it enhances trust and safety in clinical decision support, potentially setting a new standard for explainable and reliable AI-generated reports. On ChestMNIST, the classifier achieves a macro AUROC of 0.729 and ranks better than chance on all 14 labels, with precision 1.6 to 6.8 times that of a random ranker. However, at the default 0.5 threshold it emits no positive prediction for 11 of the labels, and its Brier score of 0.045 is only slightly better than the 0.047 of a predictor that ignores the image, highlighting the issue of class imbalance.

## [TRACE-Bench: A Capability-Oriented Benchmark for Multi-Reference Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16765) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TRACE-Bench introduces a capability-oriented benchmark that decomposes multi-reference image generation into four atomic operators: Anchor, Disentangle, Apply, and Compose. It comprises approximately 1,600 evaluation cases built from 631 formula templates and around 4,000 reference images, with an operator-aligned evaluation protocol and diagnostic tree analysis. This benchmark addresses a gap in existing multi-reference image generation benchmarks, which are organized around predefined task types and lack diagnostic value. By formalizing atomic operators, it enables per-capability scoring and recursive failure localization, providing insights that holistic scoring misses, such as the primary bottleneck being disentanglement and attribute binding rather than scene composition. The benchmark includes slot counts from 1 to 8, with 631 formula templates and around 4,000 reference images spanning diverse artistic styles and real-world subjects. Evaluation of 9 leading models shows that even the best model scores only 0.74 on attribute fidelity, highlighting the difficulty of attribute binding.

The paper introduces SAPO (Step-Aligned Policy Optimization), a novel reinforcement learning method that assigns a separate group-relative advantage to each reasoning step (a thinking block paired with an SID token) instead of broadcasting a single advantage to the whole response. Experiments on three real-world recommendation datasets show that SAPO stabilizes RL training and consistently outperforms existing generative recommendation baselines. This work addresses a critical limitation in reasoning-based generative recommendation: the credit assignment problem when exact-match feedback is sparse. By aligning rewards with individual reasoning steps, SAPO improves training efficiency and recommendation accuracy, potentially advancing the integration of RL with structured generation in large-scale recommender systems. SAPO computes a separate group-relative advantage for each reasoning step and applies it only to the corresponding thinking block and SID token, rather than using a single outcome-reward with exact-match feedback. The method shows the largest gains in scenarios where sparse exact-match feedback makes reasoning-step credit assignment important, suggesting that RL objectives should mirror the decoder's output decomposition.

## [Rethinking Token-wise Feature Caching: DuCa Accelerates Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.18911) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper challenges the necessity of computing 'important' tokens in token-wise feature caching for diffusion transformers, and proposes a dual feature caching strategy (DuCa) that alternates aggressive and conservative caching with random token selection. Experiments on DiT, PixArt, FLUX, and OpenSora show significant acceleration improvements over previous token-wise caching methods. This work provides counter-intuitive insights that could reshape how feature caching is designed for diffusion transformers, potentially leading to more efficient image and video generation. It challenges the common assumption that important tokens must always be computed, which could influence future acceleration techniques in the generative AI ecosystem. DuCa performs aggressive caching and conservative caching iteratively, and selects tokens for computing randomly, which is shown to be more effective than selecting 'important' tokens. The paper demonstrates that consistently computing selected important tokens is unnecessary and sometimes even inferior to random selection.

This paper re-evaluates that approach and introduces DuCa as an alternative.

The paper introduces Bactrainus, a modular selector-reader framework for multi-hop question answering that separates paragraph selection, supporting-sentence identification, and answer generation. It demonstrates that supplying full candidate context instead of gold supporting facts reduces answer token-overlap F1 by 17-21 points, showing that scale alone does not remove context sensitivity. This work addresses a significant bottleneck in multi-hop QA—the vulnerability of large language models to irrelevant context—and provides practical insights for optimizing LLMs. The modular framework and thorough ablations offer an auditable, explicitly supervised evidence interface that could improve performance and interpretability in complex reasoning tasks. The strongest configuration achieves 89.01 answer F1 and 79.70 joint F1 on the HotpotQA distractor setting. The study uses Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct readers with parameter-efficient adaptation, and finds that reader adaptation and sentence-level evidence control yield the largest differences, while decomposition and rationale-supervision variants produce smaller, recipe-dependent changes.

This paper identifies a bias in influence-based instruction tuning data selection that favors high-influence tasks, and proposes BIDS, a Balanced and Influential Data Selection algorithm that normalizes influence scores and iteratively selects examples for the most underrepresented task. Experiments with Llama-3 and Mistral-v0.3 on seven benchmarks show that BIDS consistently outperforms existing methods, and training on a 15% subset can even surpass full-dataset training. This work addresses a critical limitation in influence-based data selection for instruction tuning, which is widely used to improve LLM performance. By proposing a balanced selection strategy, BIDS can help practitioners achieve more balanced capabilities across tasks, potentially leading to more robust and versatile LLMs with less training data. The paper reveals that influence-based methods inherently favor tasks with higher influence scores, which not only hurts performance on other tasks but also on the high-influence tasks themselves. BIDS normalizes influence scores and iteratively selects the example with the highest influence on the most underrepresented task, and experiments show it outperforms both influence-based and non-influence-based baselines.

## [PrivateDFL: Transparent Noise Accounting Boosts Privacy-Preserving Decentralized Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10691) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PrivateDFL introduces a transparent noise accountant for decentralized federated learning that tracks cumulative perturbation, allowing each client to add only minimal incremental noise to satisfy its privacy budget. This approach proves that cumulative noise grows logarithmically with clients and rounds, improving accuracy by up to 62% and reducing latency and energy consumption by over 100 times compared to baselines. This work addresses a critical inefficiency in decentralized federated learning where existing methods add worst-case noise at every step, degrading model accuracy. By providing a tighter privacy-accuracy trade-off, PrivateDFL makes privacy-preserving collaborative learning more practical for sensitive domains like healthcare and human-activity monitoring. PrivateDFL pairs hyperdimensional computing with a transparent noise accountant, proving that every transmitted model satisfies the target privacy guarantee. Across image, speech, and wearable-sensor benchmarks under both IID and non-IID data, it surpasses centrally trained Transformer and deep neural network baselines, improving accuracy by 16% on images, 62% on speech, and 14% on wearable sensing, while reducing inference latency by up to 119 times and energy consumption by up to 143 times.

Differential privacy offers formal protection by adding noise, but existing decentralized methods lack visibility into noise already injected, leading to excessive perturbation. Hyperdimensional computing is a neuro-inspired approach that represents information as high-dimensional vectors, which can be efficient for edge devices. A noise accountant tracks cumulative privacy loss, enabling minimal noise addition while maintaining guarantees.

## [Robust Privacy: Certified Robustness for Inference-Stage Privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.17360) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces Robust Privacy (RP), a new inference-stage privacy notion that uses certified robustness to provably limit an adversary's advantage in distinguishing inputs from released predictions. It also formalizes Robust Attribute Privacy (RAP) and demonstrates significant reductions in attribute inference and model inversion attack success rates. This work addresses a critical gap in privacy-preserving machine learning by targeting the inference interface as a side channel, offering formal guarantees that complement existing training-stage methods like DP-SGD. It could enable more practical privacy-utility tradeoffs, as RP retains high accuracy while drastically reducing attack success rates, potentially influencing future privacy standards in ML deployment. The paper proves that under (R, α)-Robust Privacy, any adversary has at most α/2 advantage in distinguishing an input from others within distance R. Experiments show RP reduces model inversion attack success rate from 73% to 4%, and retains 98.4% accuracy at 21% ASR, outperforming DP-SGD and randomized response in the privacy-utility tradeoff space.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 18, 04:00

**Background**: Certified robustness provides formal guarantees that a model's prediction remains invariant within a neighborhood of an input, typically achieved through techniques like randomized smoothing. Inference-stage privacy concerns leakage of sensitive information through the model's outputs, which can be exploited by adversaries for attribute inference or model inversion attacks. Traditional privacy methods like DP-SGD focus on training-stage privacy, but this work shifts focus to the inference interface.

## [Credit Fairness: A New Fairness Notion for Repeated Resource Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.17944) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces credit fairness, a new property for repeated resource allocation among agents with time-varying demands and capped linear utilities. It shows that credit fairness can be achieved with either Pareto efficiency or strategyproofness, but not both under anonymity, and proposes a mechanism that is credit fair and Pareto efficient. This work addresses a fundamental tension in mechanism design for shared resource pools, offering a new fairness criterion that strengthens sharing incentives. It is relevant to multi-agent systems and cloud computing, where repeated allocation of resources among users is common. The paper proves that the max-min mechanism satisfies sharing incentives, strategyproofness, and Pareto efficiency but can lead to large disparities in total resources received. Credit fairness gives priority to agents who lent resources in early rounds to recoup them later, and the proposed mechanism is evaluated in a computational resource-sharing setting.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 18, 04:00

**Background**: In repeated resource allocation, agents have time-varying demands and capped linear utilities, meaning each agent's utility is linear in the amount of resource received up to a cap. Max-min fairness aims to maximize the minimum utility among agents, but it may not ensure fairness in total received resources over time. Credit fairness is a novel property that addresses this by tracking resource lending and borrowing across rounds.

## [LoRA-CRAFT: Cross-Layer Tucker Decomposition for Ultra-Efficient Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17510) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LoRA-CRAFT (CRAFT) introduces a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that applies frozen Tucker decomposition to pre-trained attention weights stacked across transformer layers, training only small square adaptation matrices on the resulting frozen factors. It achieves competitive performance with LoRA on LLaMA3-8B while using hundreds of times fewer parameters. This method bridges two lines of PEFT research—decomposing gradient updates versus pre-trained weights—by applying HOSVD directly to cross-layer weight tensors, potentially enabling more efficient fine-tuning of large models. Its efficiency advantage grows with model scale, which is crucial for adapting increasingly large LLMs with limited resources. CRAFT performs full Tucker decomposition via Higher-Order SVD (HOSVD) on pre-trained weights organized as 3D tensors across layers, freezing all factors and adapting via lightweight transformations. Experiments on GLUE with RoBERTa-base/large and commonsense reasoning with LLaMA2-7B/LLaMA3-8B show competitive performance with extremely low adaptation parameters, e.g., exceeding LoRA's average accuracy on LLaMA3-8B with hundreds of times fewer parameters.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Aug 18, 04:00

**Background**: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods adapt large pre-trained models by updating only a small fraction of parameters, making fine-tuning more feasible. Tucker decomposition, also known as higher-order singular value decomposition (HOSVD), generalizes matrix SVD to tensors, decomposing a tensor into factor matrices and a core tensor. Existing tensor-based PEFT methods like LoTR and SuperLoRA decompose gradient updates, while PiSSA applies SVD to pre-trained weights per layer; CRAFT combines these ideas by decomposing cross-layer weight tensors directly.

## [SymbolicLight V1: Spike-Gated Dual-Path Language Model with High Sparsity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21333) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SymbolicLight V1 introduces a spike-gated dual-path language model that combines binary Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) dynamics with a continuous residual stream. Trained from scratch on a 3B-token bilingual corpus, it achieves a token-weighted perplexity of 8.904 (mean) at over 89% activation sparsity, with energy consumption of 2,848 mJ/token on an RTX 2080 Ti. This work demonstrates that spiking language models can achieve competitive perplexity while maintaining high activation sparsity, potentially enabling more energy-efficient NLP inference. It bridges spiking neural networks and language modeling, offering a new direction for efficient AI models that could reduce the carbon footprint of large-scale deployments. The model uses a Dual-Path SparseTCAM mixer that couples a first-order exponential-decay state with windowed local attention on the continuous residual stream. It achieves a token-weighted mean PPL of 8.904 (7.7% above GPT-2 201M's 8.27) and shows no clear accuracy separation on five zero-shot benchmarks, while producing lower 4-gram repetition under certain sampling settings.

## [Compositional Boundaries for Density Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05871) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper establishes a compositional boundary for hierarchical order-invariant fusion of weighted probability densities, proving that normalized weighted linear pooling is the unique continuous binary rule under certain conditions. It also reveals that endpoint-to-candidate f-divergence balancing has a local geometry that obstructs schedule-independent fusion. This work provides a rigorous algebraic characterization of when hierarchical fusion of probabilistic models is order-invariant, which is crucial for distributed uncertainty-management systems. It distinguishes exact schedule-independent fusion from global aggregation objectives and local approximation heuristics, potentially guiding the design of more reliable fusion algorithms in AI/ML and systems research. The paper shows that within the class of continuous binary rules with additive output weights and weight-only coefficients, order-invariant hierarchical execution characterizes normalized weighted linear pooling, with norm-induced segment balancing realizing the corresponding coefficient. It also demonstrates that smooth endpoint-to-candidate f-divergence balancing has a quadratic expansion that induces square-root effective weights, explaining why pairwise solvability alone is insufficient for schedule-independent fusion.

The paper introduces Speculative Rollback Correction (SRC), a branch-level imitation learning framework for resettable web agent environments. SRC uses fixed-horizon speculative execution and teacher review to correct errors, collecting 977 verifier-passing trajectories and 9,183 next-action examples on WebArena-Infinity. This work addresses the critical challenge of when to intervene in imitation learning for interactive agents, balancing delayed and premature intervention. It offers a practical method to improve training stability and maintain behavioral diversity, which could enhance the performance of web agents in real-world tasks. SRC performs fixed-horizon branch review: the student executes a short speculative segment before teacher review, and the teacher localizes the first harmful deviation only when local progress breaks. Rollback preserves useful prefixes, and successful rollouts are filtered by a hard verifier and stored in a quality-diversity archive. The code is available at https://github.com/LongkunHao/SRC_gui_agent.
